headline: Four AI Agents Fixed a GitHub Issue without human intervention, writing and testing code
summary: A fully autonomous AI system successfully reads GitHub issues, understands codebases, writes and tests code, gets it reviewed by another AI, and opens a pull request, all without human input.
details: A developer created an autonomous AI system that can read a GitHub issue, understand a codebase, write working code, run tests, get the code reviewed by another AI, and open a pull request. The entire process requires no human intervention.

The project was initially thought to be too ambitious for one person using free API tiers. However, the system successfully completed its first full run, demonstrating its capability to handle software development tasks autonomously.

The system addresses the inefficiency of simple bug fixes, which often involve more time in context switching and administrative tasks than actual coding. It aims to allow developers to describe a problem in plain English and walk away.

The 'Architect' agent reads the repository, identifies relevant files, understands the codebase structure, and formulates a concrete implementation plan. This plan is then posted as a comment on the GitHub issue for transparency.

The 'Coder' agent operates within a fresh cloud sandbox, cloning the repository and writing code based on the Architect's plan. It runs linters, commits changes, and executes the test suite, attempting fixes if tests fail.

The 'Reviewer' agent performs a line-by-line review of the git diff, checking for common vulnerabilities like hardcoded secrets, SQL injection risks, and missing input validation. It either approves the code or sends it back with specific feedback.
Finally, the 'PR Agent' creates a draft pull request on GitHub, complete with a detailed description of the changes made, the rationale behind them, and the output from the test runs.

This entire process can run in approximately four minutes for simple feature requests. The system differentiates itself by using completely separate AI agents, each with distinct roles and tools, operating without knowledge of each other's internal reasoning.

The system utilizes real tools and environments: Groq provides Llama 3.1 access for agent processing, E2B offers cloud sandboxes for code execution, LangGraph manages the agent graph, FastAPI serves the backend, and Next.js streams live logs.

Developing the system involved overcoming challenges such as models attempting to call non-existent tools, hitting token limits, sandbox boot failures, and incorrect test runner logic for different programming languages. These issues were resolved through iterative refinement.

In a real-world test, the system successfully added a high score tracker to a JavaFX Brick Breaker game. The Architect analyzed 800 lines of Java code, and the Coder created a new ScoreManager.java file, wired it into the game, and compiled the project.

headline: GrapheneOS offers strong defenses against data extraction from locked devices
summary: The custom Android OS heavily builds upon Android 17's security features and the most secure hardware, currently Pixel devices, with Motorola support coming in 2027.
details: GrapheneOS provides robust data extraction defenses, leveraging Android 17's security and Pixel hardware. It's set to expand its support to Motorola devices in 2027, thanks to partnerships with Motorola Mobility and Qualcomm.
Disk encryption is a core protection, making direct data breaches extremely difficult. Attackers typically need to exploit the OS in an After First Unlock state or brute-force the PIN/password.

Android 16 QPR2 mandates a secure element with escalating rate limiting for unlock attempts, reaching 41 days after 15 failures. GrapheneOS exclusively supports devices implementing this latest generation secure element.

These secure elements also feature insider attack resistance, requiring owner authentication for firmware updates. This prevents any government or malicious actor from coercing a firmware update to remove rate limits.

GrapheneOS extends password limits from 16 to 128 characters, enabling high-entropy diceware passphrases. It also introduces an optional 2nd factor fingerprint PIN, reducing fingerprint attempts to 5 for enhanced security.

The OS significantly improves exploit protections with hardened memory allocators and hardware memory tagging (MTE). It also adds specialized physical access defenses, like blocking new USB connections by default when locked.

A locked device auto-reboot timer, shipped by GrapheneOS in 2021 and now defaulted to 18 hours, returns devices to Before First Unlock state. This feature, which includes memory zeroing, has also been adopted by iOS 18.1 and Android 16.

GrapheneOS enhances multi-user security by allowing secondary users and Private Space to return to Before First Unlock state without a reboot. A duress PIN/password feature also enables device wiping when entered.
